title: Child Deportation Orders Nearly Double in Newark Court as DOJ Accelerates Immigration Backlog Push
excerpt: Legal advocates say children as young as 11 are being funnelled into mass hearings without attorneys, with 81% now receiving deportation orders compared to 43% under the Biden administration.
body:
• In the last six months, 81% of children who received a case outcome in Newark's federal immigration court were ordered to leave the U.S., nearly double the 43% rate under the Biden administration.
  • Hearings in Newark now include as many as 50 immigrants per session, with children being lumped into adult proceedings rather than heard on the juvenile docket.
  • Only 56% of children in U.S. immigration courts have legal representation. Those without lawyers face a 77% asylum denial rate.
  • Policy changes to Special Immigrant Juvenile Status mean children with approved federal protections can still be removed while waiting for visa processing.

The Numbers

The federal immigration court in Newark, New Jersey — the state's only immigration court for children — is processing cases at a pace that legal advocates describe as unprecedented. In the last six months, 81% of children who received a case outcome were ordered to depart from the United States, compared to 43% in the final six months of the Biden administration, according to data from the Vera Institute of Justice's Advancing Universal Representation Initiative, as reported by NorthJersey.com.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=Ug_H8WQ-0H8

"It feels like Newark is the new Texas," said Priscilla Monico Marín, executive director of the New Jersey Consortium for Immigrant Children, which provides legal representation for undocumented children. "You have this disturbing trend of many, many kids being ordered removed from the United States."

Mass Hearings and Rushed Outcomes

Legal advocacy groups report that hearings in the Newark court now include as many as 50 immigrants summoned for a single session. Some hearings originally scheduled for 2028 have been moved forward to 2026. In what advocates call an alarming departure from established practice, children are being heard alongside adults rather than on the dedicated juvenile docket, NorthJersey.com reported.

"Suddenly, the way the court is operating, it feels like kids are on this expedited assembly line toward deportation," Monico Marín said. "Cases are being pushed through. Kids are being given very short continuances to return, and that's coupled with a shortage of legal providers."

A Justice Department spokesperson told NorthJersey.com that "reducing the immigration court backlog remains one of the highest priorities for this administration" and that the government is prioritising "the timely completion of all cases."

Children Without Lawyers

Under U.S. law, there is no right to legal counsel in immigration court — for adults or children. Only 56% of children in American immigration courts have legal representation, according to Vera's research. The consequences are stark: 77% of asylum seekers without an attorney were denied asylum between 2020 and 2025, per Tracreports.org.

"The power dynamic between an unrepresented child and a seasoned ICE attorney before the court, for children who are eligible for relief, is itself a huge disadvantage."

— Priscilla Monico Marín, New Jersey Consortium for Immigrant Children

In a June hearing observed by NorthJersey.com, two school-age sisters appeared before Judge Shana Chen seeking asylum. Their father, who had accompanied them to the courthouse, did not enter the building because he feared arrest by ICE. An 11-year-old boy and his 20-year-old brother from Mexico appeared without legal representation; the older brother told the judge they were waitlisted for an attorney.

Special Immigrant Juvenile Status Under Threat

The Trump administration changed its policy on Special Immigrant Juvenile Status in April, removing a key protection for endangered, abandoned, or abused children. Previously, children who obtained this federal status had their immigration court cases closed or received long continuances while their visas were processed. Under the new rules, even children with legally approved status are not protected from removal while waiting, Monico Marín told NorthJersey.com.

"It's devastating, because SIJS is federal law, put in place by Congress with legislative intent to protect these children," she said. "Those visas take a long time. Even after you're approved, it takes years before you can adjust and apply for a green card."

What to Watch

The acceleration of child deportation proceedings in Newark mirrors a national pattern reported by Reuters in April, where children as young as four were being brought to court repeatedly, sometimes without legal help. Whether congressional action — such as the Fairness for Immigrant Families Act recently introduced by Sen. Cortez Masto — can reverse these trends will depend on political dynamics that currently favour enforcement over due process protections.
nri_angle: The collapse of due process protections in immigration courts affects all immigrant communities, including South Asian families navigating the system. The shortage of legal representation and accelerated timelines are systemic issues that cross ethnic lines.
author: Diaspora Desk
